name: Strait of Hormuz
limits: EIA: deep and wide enough for the largest crude tankers; traffic separation scheme runs through Omani waters.

f.n: Pre-war level per EIA STEO, as reported by Rigzone
About one-fifth of global LNG trade, mainly Qatar

alternatives.label: Saudi East-West pipeline to Yanbu (Red Sea) plus UAE Abu Dhabi-Fujairah pipeline
alternatives.note: Goreh-Jask (Iran) about 0.3 mb/d effective; a planned UAE Jebel Dhanna-Fujairah line of 1.5 mb/d by 2027. Yanbu route depends on Red Sea security.

summary: The only sea exit from the Persian Gulf, carrying about a fifth of world oil consumption and roughly a fifth of global LNG trade in 2024. Since the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February 2026 it has been largely closed to commercial traffic, the largest oil supply disruption on record.

name: Strait of Malacca
limits: Shallow sections constrain the largest tankers. Wikipedia (Malaccamax, 2026) gives the strait as about 25 m deep and the Malaccamax design draught as about 20.5 m, for a ship of about 333 m by 60 m and 300,000 dwt; not stated in the EIA page.

alternatives.label: Lombok / Makassar and Sunda Straits
alternatives.note: Deeper Indonesian routes for ultra-large vessels, adding distance.

alternatives.label: Myanmar-China crude pipeline
alternatives.note: Capacity not stated in EIA source.

summary: The shortest sea route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, carrying the largest oil flow of any chokepoint and most Gulf crude, LNG, and Indonesian coal and Australian ore routes to north Asia.

name: Singapore Strait
portwatchNote: IMF PortWatch has no counter for the Singapore Strait. Its nearest counter is the Malacca Strait, shown on the Strait of Malacca page.
summary: Eastern end of the Strait of Malacca; very high local traffic density.
parallelNote: Ships can also pass south of Singapore through the Riau islands and the Durian Strait, about 130 nm longer from Samarinda to Paradip; the atlas counts them at Singapore.

name: Sunda Strait
summary: Indonesian strait between Java and Sumatra, an alternative to Malacca for some Indian Ocean to South China Sea traffic, notably from the Cape; heavy volcanic and shallow hazards limit size.
limits: Shallow: Wikipedia (Sunda Strait, 2026) gives a minimum depth of about 20 m in parts of its north-east end.

name: Lombok Strait
limits: Deep water suitable for fully laden Capesize and VLCC vessels; Wikipedia (Lombok Strait, 2026) gives a depth of about 250 m.
summary: Deep-water route between Bali and Lombok used by Capesizes and VLCCs too deep for Malacca, and an alternative if Malacca is restricted. Preferred for Australian iron ore and coal to north Asia.
parallelNote: Ships can also take the Alas Strait, between Lombok and Sumbawa, about 50 nm longer on the Port Hedland to Qingdao run; the atlas counts them at Lombok.

name: Suez Canal
limits: Max draft about 20.1 m (66 ft) for Suezmax; larger ballast VLCCs transit, laden VLCCs need partial lightering or the SUMED pipeline. Check Suez Canal Authority for current limits.

alternatives.label: Cape of Good Hope
alternatives.note: Main alternative. The extra distance depends on the voyage: the typical detour above is measured on the atlas's mapped lanes.

alternatives.label: SUMED pipeline
alternatives.note: EIA lists 2.5 mb/d capacity, Ain Sukhna to Sidi Kerir.

summary: Shortcut between the Mediterranean and Red Sea carrying tankers, LNG, boxships and Black Sea/Mediterranean cargoes to Asia. Traffic collapsed after the Houthi attacks of 2023 and has been recovering in 2026 as carriers return.

name: Bab el-Mandeb
limits: About 18 miles wide at the narrowest point, with the shipping lanes in the Perim channel; no draft limit for oil tankers.

alternatives.label: Cape of Good Hope
alternatives.note: Main alternative; no pipeline bypass listed by EIA.

summary: Southern entrance to the Red Sea, connecting Suez to the Indian Ocean. Targeted by Houthi attacks since November 2023 and again by the Houthi blockade of Saudi Arabia in 2026; now also carrying Saudi bypass crude from Yanbu.

name: Panama Canal
limits: Two lock systems: Panamax (about 32.3 m beam) and Neopanamax (since 2016, larger LNG and LPG carriers). Draft and slot limits vary with Gatun Lake levels.

trafficRef.n: Fiscal year ending 30 Sep 2025; 3,342 Neopanamax, 10,062 Panamax

alternatives.label: Cape Horn / Magellan / Drake Passage
alternatives.note: EIA says adds up to about 8,000 miles.

alternatives.label: Cape of Good Hope or Suez
alternatives.note: Alternative from US Gulf to Asia.

alternatives.label: Trans-Panama pipeline
alternatives.note: 0.864 mb/d capacity, about 0.4 mb/d moved in 2024-25 (EIA).

summary: Connects Atlantic and Pacific, key for US Gulf LPG, grain and products to Asia and west-coast South America, and for containers. Drought in 2023-24 limited transits; FY2025 transits recovered to 13,404.

name: Turkish Straits (Bosphorus and Dardanelles)
limits: Narrowest point under half a nautical mile; Bosphorus about 17 nm, Dardanelles about 37 nm. Daylight-only transit for large tankers (Turkish regulations); no draft limit is given in the sources the atlas uses.

alternatives.label: BTC and CPC pipelines
alternatives.note: BTC to Ceyhan and Iraq-Turkey pipelines; capacities not in the EIA source.

summary: Only outlet of the Black Sea, carrying Russian and CPC (Kazakh) crude, Russian and Ukrainian grain and Black Sea products. Large tankers face daylight-only and traffic-control rules; LNG carriers may not transit.

name: Danish Straits
portwatchNote: IMF PortWatch counts the Oresund only. It has no counter for the Great Belt, the other main passage of the Danish Straits, so this series is not the traffic of the Danish Straits as a whole.
limits: Shallow, draft-restricted passages in the Great Belt and Oresund. Wikipedia (Drogden, 2026) gives the Drogden channel (Oresund) a depth of about 8 m for passing ships; this is a channel depth, not an official draught limit. No Great Belt figure is given in the sources the atlas uses.

alternatives.label: Kiel Canal
alternatives.note: About 0.2 mb/d in 1H25, small tankers and mainly products (EIA).

summary: Exit for Baltic exports, notably Russian Primorsk and Ust-Luga crude and products, and a feeder for Baltic coal and grain.

name: Strait of Gibraltar
summary: Gateway between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean, linking Suez-bound and Cape-diverted traffic with Europe.

name: Dover Strait
limits: Deep-draft route (the Dover Strait traffic separation scheme); the strait is about 20 m deep over its highest banks and 68 m in its deepest part (Wikipedia, Strait of Dover, 2026).
summary: Busiest strait in the world by transits, linking the North Sea to the English Channel for ARA and Baltic traffic.
parallelNote: Ships can also reach the North Sea north of Scotland, about 160 nm longer from Corpus Christi to Rotterdam; the atlas counts them at Dover.

name: Cape of Good Hope
summary: Not a chokepoint but the main alternative to Suez/Bab el-Mandeb; also the usual route for ultra-large vessels. Traffic rose sharply after the Red Sea crisis began.

name: Cape Horn
portwatchNote: IMF PortWatch has no counter for Cape Horn. It counts the Magellan Strait, the sheltered passage to the north: that series is shown here under its own name.
summary: Southernmost tip of South America; alternative to the Panama Canal and Magellan Strait for oversized vessels, with harsh weather.

name: Taiwan Strait
summary: Main north-south route for China-Japan-Korea trade, container and crude flows.

name: Korea Strait
summary: Link between the East China Sea and the Sea of Japan between Korea and Japan.
parallelNote: Ships from the Pacific to northern China can also pass south of Japan, 1 to 4.5% longer (about 245 nm from Callao to Qingdao); the atlas counts their cargo in the up-to figure only.

name: Makassar Strait
summary: One of the 28 passages counted by IMF PortWatch. Traffic only: the atlas's mapped lanes are not tagged with this passage and it holds no published flow statistics for it.
parallelNote: Ships can also go by the Ombai Strait and the Banda and Molucca Seas, about 110 nm longer on the Port Hedland to Qingdao run; the atlas counts them at Makassar.

name: Luzon Strait
summary: One of the 28 passages counted by IMF PortWatch. Traffic only: the atlas's mapped lanes are not tagged with this passage and it holds no published flow statistics for it.
parallelNote: Ships can also cross the Philippine archipelago, about 270 nm longer for a Capesize from Newcastle to Kaohsiung; the atlas counts them at the Luzon Strait.
